settings.title: a workshop in hackney
settings.body: Design engineers James Marr and Ian McMillan open the UK's first bamboo bike workshop. The Guardian covers it. They never sell a finished bicycle — they teach people to build their own.
settings.image_alt: The first Bamboo Bicycle Club workshop, frames on the bench and the club logo painted on the wall

settings.title: the design museum, and a first
settings.body: London's Design Museum exhibits the bike — the first bamboo frame built with 3D-printed lugs. The home-build kit starts shipping worldwide; builders make frames at their kitchen tables.

settings.title: kevin mccloud's green heroes
settings.body: Selected at Grand Designs Live as one of Kevin McCloud’s Green Heroes for sustainable design.
settings.image_alt: Bamboo Bicycle Club's stand at Grand Designs Live

settings.title: the cycling world takes a proper look
settings.body: The Global Cycling Network puts a bamboo frame through its paces in “Are Bamboo Bikes Actually Any Good?”, the public edit of the GCN+ film “Bamboo Bike: Fad or Future”.

settings.title: a governor asks for accreditation
settings.body: HMP Lowdham Grange will only run the course if it is accredited. James builds one from scratch — OCN London Level 2, Workshop Skills and Sustainable Manufacturing — and a frame-building workshop goes in behind the wall.
settings.image_alt: The frame-building workshop inside HMP Lowdham Grange — benches and wall-mounted jigs, empty

settings.title: the year the work was recognised
settings.body: Bamboo Mobility Project CIC is incorporated in February. In September the Financial Times profiles the prison programme and Investec’s Beyond Business backs it with £24,000 from 148 applicants. Inside Time carries it in November.

settings.title: craft over consumption
settings.body: A bike you build yourself is a bike you never throw away. We teach making, not buying.
settings.evidence: Architect Taro Tsuruta has ridden the frame he built for ten years. It is still his daily bike.
settings.image_alt: A loaded bamboo touring bike parked beside a waymarker on open moorland

settings.title: grown, not mined
settings.body: Bamboo regrows in 3–5 years and recycles fully. Sustainability is the material, not the marketing.
settings.evidence: Our frames were tested to BS ISO 22157 at Swansea University. The material is a grass — cut it, and it regrows from the same root.
settings.image_alt: Cut and mitred bamboo tubes on a workbench beside a carpenter pencil

settings.title: open to everyone
settings.body: From weekend workshops to prisons and schools, our goal is to put making within reach of people who'd never otherwise get the chance.
settings.evidence: Jon had the use of one hand. We adapted every step so the build stayed in his hands rather than ours — he left with a frame he had built himself.
settings.image_alt: Gloved hands wrapping and binding a bamboo frame joint on the workbench

settings.title: ten years on, still his daily ride.
settings.blurb: Architect Taro Tsuruta built his own frame after reading about us. A decade later it is still the bike he rides.

settings.title: 8,288 miles down the Andes, on a frame she built herself.
settings.blurb: Kate Rawles built her bike with us, then rode the length of South America on it.

settings.title: london to singapore, on bamboo they built themselves.
settings.blurb: Two doctors rode 22,000km across Europe and Asia on frames they made in our workshop.

settings.title: five years commuting, then a repaint — not a replacement.
settings.blurb: Claire rode hers across London every day for about five years, and came back to tidy the paint and add panniers.

settings.title: one hand, one frame — and he built it himself.
